evidence.text: For compact medical LLMs, medical capability and deployment efficiency can be optimized jointly: high-quality synthetic supervision and staged post-training build accuracy, while length-aware alignment and quantization reduce generation and memory costs for private on-device use. We test this thesis by constructing the MedPsy 1 1 In MedPsy, “Med” denotes the medical specialization, while “Psy” is the shared suffix used across our organization’s model families, inspired by psychohistory in Isaac Asimov’s fiction rather than psychology. family of two text-only medical models, MedPsy -1.7B and MedPsy -4B 2 2 Models and supporting artifacts are available at https://huggingface.co/collections/qvac/medpsy . , on top of Qwen3 backbones [ 3 ] with a four-stage post-training recipe (two Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) stages over a synthetic medical corpus built from public Genesis III biology/medicine seed prompts [ 4 ] and newly generated health seeds derived from FineFineWeb [ 5 ] , then two Reinforcement Learning (RL) stages with hard-sample mining inspired by Fleming-R1 [ 6 ] ), and we evaluate them across eight benchmark suites spanning clinical exams (MedQA-USMLE [ 7 ] , MedMCQA [ 8 ] ), health literacy (MMLU-Health, MMLU-Pro Health [ 9 , 10 ] ), expert reasoning (MedXpertQA [ 11 ] ), biomedical research (PubMedQA [ 12 ] ), underserved-region medicine (AfriMedQA [ 13 ] ), and real-world clinical scenarios (HealthBench and HealthBench-Hard [ 14 ] ).

evidence.text: These limitations point to several directions for future work. The recipe should be extended to multilingual and multimodal medical settings, and evaluation should move beyond the current benchmark suite. In particular, compact medical models need stronger open-ended evaluations, safety benchmarks, and medical error detection tests before their behavior can be understood in higher-risk clinical scenarios. Within this scope, MedPsy shows that compact, text-only medical LLMs (1.7B and 4B) can match or surpass much larger medical models: MedPsy -4B matches MedGemma-27B on closed-ended benchmarks at 6.75 \times smaller scale, and both sizes surpass it on HealthBench-Hard. Both run fully locally within 5 GB of peak RAM on the tested laptop and smartphone, where shorter generations cut median latency and estimated energy per answer by 75%. A controlled synthetic-data pipeline, a broad-then-focused SFT curriculum, and hard-sample RL deliver strong medical accuracy and improved token efficiency ( 1.7 – 3.2\times fewer generated tokens) at small scale. The quantization study further shows that Q4_K_M keeps aggregate score within one point of BF16 at a 68–69% smaller footprint, while very low precision exposes a clear capacity-vs-precision trade-off. Overall, MedPsy suggests that for compact medical LLMs, data quality, staged post-training, and alignment design dominate parameter scale, and medical capability and deployment efficiency can be optimized jointly.

evidence.text: We explored several data mixtures and post-training methodologies before settling on the recipe used for the final MedPsy models. In total, about 10M synthetic rows of medical and healthcare supervision were generated for the final synthetic corpus. The recipe organizes the data into a two-stage curriculum : a broad-coverage corpus (Corpus 1) followed by a smaller, higher-value clinical-QA corpus (Corpus 2). The two corpora play complementary roles in the SFT curriculum (Sec. 4 ). Two principles guided the data construction throughout these ablations: Synthetic datasets. Corpus 1 utilizes broad synthetic prompts derived from two primary sources. First, we extracted the question and answer option fields from four public Genesis III subsets [ 4 ] : college_medicine , professional_medicine , college_biology , and high_school_biology . Second, following [ 4 ] , we use Fleming-R1-32B [ 6 ] to generate four multiple-choice questions (MCQs) for each document in the FineFineWeb health sub-domain [ 5 ] . We selected Fleming-R1-32B as it achieves strong performance on closed-ended medical tasks while offering higher throughput than larger teacher models. Corpus 2 instead utilizes train splits from focused open-source medical QA datasets as higher-value clinical prompts. Together, these broad synthetic and focused public-train prompts are used as seeds to generate the final synthetic training data. A single, controlled SFT target teacher. Every long-form assistant target used for supervision (chain-of-thought traces, extended rationales, decision-oriented answers) is newly generated by Baichuan-M3-235B [ 27 ] , the teacher selected in Sec. 3.2 , rather than taken from open-source assistant traces

evidence.text: Our contributions are: State-of-the-Art Efficient Models. MedPsy -4B matches MedGemma-27B on closed-ended accuracy and surpasses on HealthBench suites both MedGemma-4B (+20/+28.33) and 27B (+9.0/+15.3). Similarly, MedPsy -1.7B exceeds MedGemma-4B on closed-ended tasks and outperforms both MedGemma variants on HealthBench, achieving these leads at up to 16 \times smaller scale (Fig. 1(a) ; Sec. 5 ). Post-training recipe. We combine single-teacher synthetic supervision, broad-to-focused SFT, and easy-to-hard DAPO with deterministic failure mining. Component ablations separate the roles of SFT, DAPO’s drift-enabling changes, the overlong-response penalty, and Stage-2 mining (Sec. 5.4 ; App. A.17 ). Token efficiency for the edge. MedPsy -4B and MedPsy -1.7B achieve 3.2 \times and 1.7 \times token reductions over Qwen3 backbones, significantly lowering on-device latency (Sec. 5.5 ). This efficiency stems from RL-side compression, primarily a soft overlong-response penalty that maintains accuracy while ensuring the training curriculum remains Pareto-dominant (App. A.17.2 ). Quantized edge deployment. At Q4_K_M , both model sizes retain aggregate score within one point of BF16 while reducing disk footprint by 68–69%. On-device measurements connect MedPsy -4B’s shorter generations to 75% lower median latency and estimated energy per answer at matched quantization, while peak RAM remains below 5 GB in the tested laptop and smartphone configurations. A broader six-format study identifies a capacity-vs-precision effect at matched footprint (Sec. 5.6 ; App. A.12 ).

evidence.text: The results support our central thesis: for compact medical LLMs, medical capability and deployment efficiency can be optimized jointly. In MedPsy , broad SFT establishes medical coverage, focused SFT improves clinical reasoning, and hard-sample RL sharpens the most reasoning-heavy benchmarks (Sec. 5.4 ). The full curriculum (SFT \to SFT \to RL Stage 1 \to RL Stage 2) is also strictly Pareto-dominant over single-stage hard-only RL on token-vs-accuracy (best performance at \sim 3 – 4\times shorter response length) (App. A.17.2 ). The Easy/Moderate Stage 1 leaves the policy already compressed and high-reward before Stage 2 mining targets residual hard items, preserving response compression even in the more challenging scenarios that require longer reasoning. However, these findings should be interpreted within several important boundaries: the models are text-only ; the training data is predominantly English. Like all LLMs, the models can produce confident but incorrect medical statements; they should not be used for autonomous diagnosis or treatment. Real clinical decision support would require additional safety review, IRB-grade evaluation, prospective testing, and regulatory clearance.

evidence.text: Because our supervision is the teacher’s output, the teacher’s ceiling directly bounds the student’s. From a literature review and public medical leaderboards, we identified three strong candidates ( Baichuan-M3-235B [ 27 ] , GPT-OSS-120B [ 28 ] , and Fleming-R1-32B [ 6 ] ) and evaluated them on our benchmark suite under three independent model graders (Sec. 5.1 ). The same suite serves teacher selection and final reporting, as it directly measures the supervision quality the student distills. Baichuan-M3-235B leads with 74.83 average closed-ended accuracy (vs. 72.73/72.55), with its largest advantages on the most expert-level benchmarks (MedXpertQA: +5.61/+10.98; MMLU-Pro Health: +5.05/+2.73), and beats both alternatives by 6–12 HealthBench points across all three graders (Tables 6 , 7 ). Since the teacher’s clinical reasoning and communication quality is exactly the signal the student distills, this open-ended advantage was decisive: we use Baichuan-M3-235B as the teacher for all final MedPsy training data. A controlled student-level ablation (App. A.2 ) verifies that this choice transfers when the prompt set, base model, and training pipeline are held fixed.

evidence.text: Sample-weighted across all eight benchmarks, the 4B model achieves a 3.2 \times reduction in average response length ( 909 vs. 2,953 tokens for Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507) while improving accuracy, and the 1.7B model a 1.7 \times reduction ( 1,110 vs. 1,901 tokens for Qwen3-1.7B Thinking). Complementing these observed length reductions, an explicit thinking-budget sweep shows that MedPsy -4B retains 96.6% of its unbounded closed-ended score with a 300-token thinking cap (App. A.14 ). The 1.7B reduction is smaller because its backbone already emits shorter outputs, and on HealthBench MedPsy -1.7B writes slightly longer responses than its backbone, trading tokens for the +17 HealthBench points of Sec. 5.4 . The per-benchmark breakdown is in App. A.10 (Tab. 20 ). We decompose the RL-side compression into three independently controllable mechanisms in App. A.17.2 : vanilla GRPO with a KL anchor compresses by only \sim 6 – 20 %, switching to DAPO’s drift-enabling modifications (KL-removal and asymmetric clip-higher) brings compression to \sim 44 – 45 %, and adding the soft overlong-response penalty pushes it to the released-model \sim 65 – 66 %. The ordering of the RL stages compounds this: Stage 1 trains on items typically answerable with short reasoning, installing a low-token-budget habit; Stage 2 then pushes accuracy on hard items starting from this already-compressed checkpoint and preserves the short-reasoning habit.

evidence.text: Training stage progression. Comparison of MedPsy -1.7B (1.7B) and MedPsy -4B (4B) across all benchmarks. Avg is the closed-ended mean; HB is HealthBench Standard (CompassJudger-2-32B). Several patterns are consistent across both sizes (Table 3 ). SFT Stage 1 delivers the largest single jump (+7.53 / +4.83), confirming that broad medical exposure from Corpus 1 is the foundation; gains are most dramatic on HealthBench (+17.33 / +11.00) and MedQA-USMLE (+16.79 / +11.47). SFT Stage 2 adds focused reasoning on MedQA-USMLE (+4.79 for 1.7B), MMLU-Pro Health (+3.22 for 1.7B), and MedXpertQA (+2.49 for 4B). The two RL stages together provide the final sharpening , peaking on MedQA-USMLE (+6.29 for 1.7B) and MedMCQA (+5.02 / +2.94), the benchmarks that most reward structured clinical reasoning. Stage 2 hard-mining accounts for essentially all of the released model’s MedXpertQA lift: replacing the mined Stage-2 set with a uniformly-random subset of identical size loses 5.0 pp (4B) and 2.0 pp (1.7B) on MedXpertQA, while easy/medium benchmarks are essentially unchanged (App. A.17.1 ). HealthBench gains are installed early : SFT Stage 1 already lifts HealthBench to its final level, and the RL stages preserve it while improving closed-ended accuracy and token efficiency.

evidence.text: The Med-CoDE framework, designed to assess the reliability and accuracy of medical LLMs, operates within a domain where the potential consequences of errors are particularly significant, given the direct impact on patient care and treatment outcomes. In this work, only the publicly available standard benchmark medical QA datasets are used for training and evaluations. The Med-CoDE framework aims to enhance the evaluation of LLMs to ensure they meet rigorous standards of accuracy and reliability. However, it is essential to recognize that even well-evaluated models are not infallible and should not replace human judgment. Instead, they should be used as tools to support healthcare professionals, who must remain the final arbiters in clinical decision-making. By addressing these ethical considerations, the Med-CoDE framework can contribute to the responsible development and deployment of medical LLMs, ultimately supporting safer and more effective healthcare solutions.

evidence.text:
We extract clinical data elements as the foundational information units by cross-referencing multiple tables of the hospital and note modules of the MIMIC-IV dataset ( Johnson et al., 2023 ) , which contains hospital-wide Electronic Health Records (EHR) from 2008 to 2019 at the Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston.
First, we obtain patient profile , including gender, race, age, insurance category, language and marital status.
Second, we obtain the medical record at discharge , including major complaint, history of present illness, past medical history, social history, family history, physical exam data, allergies, and current medications at the hospital admission time. These patient status records are represented in natural language in discharge notes.
We then induce the medical record at admission by removing the sections that describe information only available after the clinical decisions (diagnoses, procedures, lab tests, and prescriptions) are made from the medical record at discharge.
Examples of those sections include discharge physical exam data, updated medication lists, and doctor’s notes/comments.
The induction is done by a rule-based NLP pipeline involving section identification, title extraction and keyword-matching. A manual screening process on 1000 sampled records iteratively updates the pipeline rules for coverage.
The correctness of all medical records at admission in the evaluation set is manually verified by a clinical NLP expert.
Third, lab test results within the admission includes lab test item, result value, units, normal range and interpretation flags.
Fourth, we identify radiology results within the admission including indications and findings of patient radiology scans.
